### Changelog

- Restored the `Automatic-Module-Name` to `guava-android`. (It, unlike, `guava-jre`, is not a proper module.) (7a04a8a955)
- For users of `guava-gwt`: Google [has moved off GWT internally](https://github.com/gwtproject/gwt-site/pull/394). We plan to continue to release `guava-gwt` for users of GWT and [J2CL](https://github.com/google/j2cl), but the artifact is no longer tested for GWT-specific issues, and we have limited resources to fix any unexpected issues that might arise. While we do not anticipate any specific problems, we can't guarantee how long support will continue.
- Increased our Android `minSdkVersion` to 23 (Marshmallow). This follows the minimum of Google's foundational Android libraries, and we expect it to have no practical impact on users. (5c23347cc1)
- Listed the JSpecify annotations as an optional dependency in our OSGi metadata. (2dfd572981)
- `cache`: Improved the handling of exceptions from compute functions in `Cache.asMap()`. (We do still [recommend](https://guava.dev/releases/snapshot-jre/api/docs/com/google/common/cache/CacheBuilder.html#prefer-caffeine-over-guava-s-caching-api-heading) using [Caffeine](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine) rather than `com.google.common.cache`.) (087f2c4a80)
- `collect`: Improved `Iterators.mergeSorted()` to preserve stability for equal elements. (4dc93be9a8)
- `math`: Added `saturatedAbs` methods to `IntMath` and `LongMath`. (ed0e518f20)
- `net`: Added `image/avif` to `MediaType`. (53344caba6)
- `testing`: Made `CollectorTester` available to Android users. (294c251079)
- `util.concurrent`: Added `Striped.custom`. (1586eb271d)

**Use Guava 33.4.8, not Guava 33.4.5**. 33.4.5 was our first attempt to modularize Guava, but we misconfigured our build, so it:

- [contains an extra copy of each of its classes](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/7743)
- [does not declare its dependencies on artifacts of annotations](https://github.com/google/guava/pull/7732)

33.4.5 (and 33.4.6) also may cause [trouble for some optimizers](https://github.com/google/guava/pull/7766) (like those commonly used for Android apps), and 33.4.7 [breaks the build of Android apps with a minSdkVersion below 26](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/7769).

All these issues are fixed by release 33.4.8. Sorry for the trouble.

- Changed `@ParametricNullness` into a no-op for Kotlin and IntelliJ. Before now, it was forcing many usages of type variables to have [platform types](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/java-interop.html#null-safety-and-platform-types), which meant that Kotlin couldn't check those usages for nullness errors. With this change, Kotlin can detect more errors. (ae36f571a2)

Today, we are releasing Guava 33.4.1 and a few other 33.4.x releases. All the releases maintain binary compatibility, but they include changes to [nullness](https://jspecify.dev/) and the module system that may be disruptive to some users.

Most users can jump straight to [33.4.8](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v33.4.8) to pick up a few small improvements with no disruption.

If you encounter trouble with 33.4.8, then read on.

### Module-system trouble

First, **use Guava 33.4.8, not Guava 33.4.5**. 33.4.5 was our first attempt to modularize Guava, but we made a few mistakes, so it:

- [contains an extra copy of each of its classes](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/7743)
- [does not declare its dependencies on artifacts of annotations](https://github.com/google/guava/pull/7732) and [misdeclares (as does 33.4.6) a few other dependencies](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/2970#issuecomment-2753313589)

33.4.5 (and 33.4.6) also may cause [trouble for some optimizers](https://github.com/google/guava/pull/7766) (like those commonly used for Android apps), and 33.4.7 [breaks the build of Android apps with a minSdkVersion below 26](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/7769).

All these issues are fixed by release 33.4.8. Sorry for the trouble.

Guava 33.4.8 (after a false start in Guava 33.4.5) changes Guava to be a [Java module](https://dev.java/learn/modules/intro/). You can still use Guava without using the module system yourself. However, if your build system automatically recognizes Guava as a module, then you may see errors. As a temporary fix, you can upgrade only to 33.4.4 while you investigate the module problems.

If you see build errors (such as `package com.google.common.collect is not visible`), try modifying your `module-info.java` to include [`requires com.google.common;`](https://dev.java/learn/modules/intro/#requiring-dependencies). 

If you see _runtime_ errors, then you may be performing reflection on Guava internals. We recommend not doing this, since Guava internals change frequently, potentially breaking such code. The module system is designed to call attention to this situation, but you can always [silence it with `--add-opens`](https://dev.java/learn/modules/add-exports-opens/#opening-packages-with---add-opens), passing the module name (`com.google.common`) and package name from your error message along with the name of the module that is accessing Guava's internals (which is also shown in the error message).

### Nullness trouble

Nullness annotations have no effect on Java itself, but they do affect nullness checkers, such as [NullAway](https://github.com/uber/NullAway/issues/1193), the Checker Framework, and Kotlin.

If you encounter only a modest number of nullness errors, we recommend upgrading straight to 33.4.8 or higher, suppressing or fixing the errors to prepare for the change.

For build errors from a Java nullness checker, you can generally silence them with `@SuppressWarnings` (docs: [NullAway](https://github.com/uber/NullAway/wiki/Suppressing-Warnings), [the Checker Framework](https://checkerframework.org/manual/#suppressing-warnings-nullness), [Error Prone](https://errorprone.info/bugpattern/NullArgumentForNonNullParameter)). Of course, we recommend inspecting at least a few new errors so that you can judge whether the errors are worth fixing instead of just suppressing.

For build errors from Kotlin, there is no supported way to suppress. (If, after reading the instructions here, you believe that one would be valuable, please [share your experiences with the Kotlin developers](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/KT-75652).) You'll instead need to change your code, often in one of the following ways:

- To insert a null value into a collection, you may need to change the collection's type, like from `Multiset<Foo>` to `Multiset<Foo?>`.
  - The same kind of change can be useful for other generic types, like in changing a `FutureCallback<Foo>` to a `FutureCallback<Foo?>` so that its `onSuccess` method can still be declared to accept a `Foo?`.
- When using our immutable collections or other null-hostile types, you may need to make the opposite change, like by using `ImmutableList<Foo>` instead of `ImmutableList<Foo?>`.
  - If you are writing your own generic API, you may need to restrict your type argument to non-null types. For example, for `ImmutableList<T>` to be valid, you may need to change your type-parameter declaration from `<T>` to [`<T: Any>`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/generics.html#upper-bounds). Occasionally, you may want to keep the type-parameter declaration as it is but change to using [`ImmutableList<T & Any>`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/generics.html#definitely-non-nullable-types).
- You can change the nullness of a type by using [`!!`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/null-safety.html#not-null-assertion-operator) or a [cast](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/typecasts.html#unsafe-cast-operator). These operators sometimes introduce a runtime check where there was not one before.
- Or there may be better fixes, such as changing the types of your own parameters to forbid `null`.

### Gradual migration

If you encounter a large number of errors when upgrading, then you may wish to upgrade your Guava version incrementally. Guava [33.4.1](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v33.4.1), [33.4.2](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v33.4.2), [33.4.3](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v33.4.3), and [33.4.4](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v33.4.4) are each one step toward improving Guava's nullness annotations. You may find it easier to upgrade one version at a time. By doing so, you can handle all problems of a particular "kind" at once. Then, once you submit the upgrade, you prevent backsliding of that kind. (Almost all problems should surface in the upgrade to 33.4.1 or the upgrade to 33.4.2.)

If you take this path, you may wish to set [`-Xjsr305=strict`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/java-interop.html#compiler-configuration) before even the first Guava upgrade. That flag may identify a subset of problems ahead of the Guava changes. Note, however, that it may also cause Kotlin to detect nullness errors in your usages of any _other_ libraries that use custom nullness annotations. If so, the flag would cause you to have to perform a _larger_ cleanup that the Guava upgrade requires, so you'll have to judge whether that flag would be helpful on net.

### Temporary emergency fallback option: Disabling current and future checking of Java APIs

In the worst case, it is possible to tell Kotlin not to produce errors for _any_ usages of JSpecify annotations, both those in Guava _and those in other libraries_ (such as [Caffeine](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/releases/tag/v3.2.0) and the forthcoming [Spring Framework 7](https://spring.io/blog/2025/03/10/null-safety-in-spring-apps-with-jspecify-and-null-away)). You can do this by setting [`-Xjspecify-annotations=warn`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew1520.html#support-for-calling-java-s-lombok-generated-methods-within-modules-that-have-kotlin-and-java-code:~:text=Xjspecify%2Dannotations). If you are considering this, we recommend instead deferring your upgrade of Guava to give yourself time to work through the nullness errors. We are making an effort not to publish a release with new APIs in the near future, so you should be able to safely defer upgrading for a while. If you do still choose to set the flag, we recommend working to remove it in the future, since it will hide more and more errors as time goes by.

### For more help

We monitor for [Guava questions on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/ask?tags=guava+java). If you believe that you are seeing a bug in a nullness checker, you can report it to the tool owners (e.g., [NullAway](https://github.com/uber/NullAway/issues/new), [the Checker Framework](https://github.com/typetools/checker-framework/issues/new)). If you believe that you are seeing a problem with these instructions or with Guava's nullness annotations, [report a bug to us](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/new/choose).
